title: Honey Fakers Were Beating the Tests. Then Europe Got Smarter.
note: The eighth 3D short (2026-11-23), made from scratch under the look bible, the notes ledger and NOT SHOWN: every line's fact is a picture a stranger can read with the sound off (a count, a size, a named thing, both sides of a comparison). One beekeeper's market day in one village. Rewritten 2026-11-23 as one chain (so/but) that passed the cold-read story gate: the old tests' one in seven, why faking pays, the fakers' labs, the sharper tests, almost half.
lines: Europe's tests caught one honey import in seven faked. The real share was worse.
Fakers stretch honey with rice syrup, which costs about a quarter as much, so every spoonful is profit.
So they pay labs to test their blends, tuning the syrup until it slips past the checks.
But EU scientists brought in a sharper test that spots rice syrup, and the tuned blends got caught.
Almost half the imports came back suspected fake, three times the old count. What's in your jar?

sources.claim: Europe's earlier tests caught about one honey import in seven
sources.says: An earlier EU wide coordinated control plan conducted in 2015-17 measured that 14 % of the analysed samples did not comply with established benchmark criteria to assess honey authenticity.

sources.claim: fakers stretch honey with syrup made from rice, which costs about a quarter as much
sources.says: The EU average unit value for imported honey was 2.17€ per kilogram (excluding honey from New Zealand) in 2021 whereas sugar syrups made from rice are available at around 0.40 – 0.60€ per kilogram.

sources.claim: so every spoonful of syrup is profit
sources.says: Diluting honey with sugar syrups provide an unfair advantage for fraudsters.

sources.claim: they pay labs to test their blends, tuning the syrup until it slips past the checks
sources.says: the regular recourse of analyses in accredited laboratories to adapt honey/sugar blends to elude possible detection by clients and official authorities prior to import operations

sources.claim: EU scientists brought sharper tests that spot rice syrup
sources.says: However, a different set of methods with improved detection capability was used in the present study, which may explain this difference.

sources.claim: the tuned blends got caught: the old test missed the new syrups, the sharper ones flagged them
sources.says: Stable carbon isotope ratio analysis by EA-IRMS (AOAC method 991.41), a method that has frequently been used in the past to detect sugar syrups made of maize starch or sugarcane, was not effective in detecting honey suspicious of being adulterated. This may indicate that sugar syrups made of maize starch or sugarcane are no longer used to extend honey and that they have been replaced totally or partially by syrups made from rice, wheat or sugar beet, for instance.

sources.claim: almost half the imports came back suspected fake
sources.says: 46% of the samples were suspicious of being adulterated with sugar syrups
This rate was considerably higher than the one obtained in 2015-17 (14%).

sets_why: one village on market day, walked by its beekeeper: the cheap stall in the square, his honey house, the cheap stall's back room where the fake is tuned, the village hall where the EU's inspectors set up their sharper test, and the alley behind the square where the stall's whole stock is tested
ideas: at the cheap stall a row of seven identical honey jars sits under a PURE HONEY sign; he slams his honey dipper on the counter, the row jumps, and only one of the seven labels flips to a red SYRUP; he squints along the other six, not convinced

outside his honey house two flagpoles stand in front of a tall price board banded every 0.50 euro a kilo; the white RICE SYRUP flag already flies at 0.50; he cranks the honey pole's winch and the gold HONEY flag climbs band by band to 2.17, four bands to the syrup's one; he looks from one to the other and rubs his hands

in the cheap stall's back room he dips his honey dipper in the blending vat and touches it to the old test box: red FAIL; he cranks the SYRUP wheel down a notch, still red; one more notch and it shows green PASS while the vat's gauge still reads mostly syrup

in the village hall the EU's new test machine with a big dial and a screen; he lets one drop of the tuned blend that passed in the back room fall into its funnel; the dial swings hard from PASS into FAKE, the screen lights RICE SYRUP and the beacon spins red

in the alley behind the square the stall's imported stock stands on a tall rack, three shelves of seven jars, one red SUSPECT in every seven from the old test; he hauls the new test's lever down, its red scan bar sweeps the shelves and two more jars in every seven spin red, three in seven, almost half; he turns to us, hands out
storyboard: 1 hook (the village square on market day, morning sun, striped awnings, crates of produce, people at the other stalls far behind; the cheap stall's counter big in front of us with a hand-painted sign PURE HONEY 2 EUROS and a row of seven identical honey jars across it; the lens low and three-quarter at the counter's end, the beekeeper whole beside it in his bee hat with his honey dipper): he looks along the row of jars, frowns at the 2 euro sign, and slams his honey dipper down on the counter; the whole row jumps and only one of the seven jars flips its label over to a big red SYRUP; he squints along the other six, not convinced, and taps the next one.

2 a quarter of the price (the yard outside his honey house: its plank wall with a deep-set window of jars on shelves, the open door onto his lit honey room, flagstones in the grass; two white flagpoles in front of a tall price board banded every 0.50 under EUROS A KILO; a red winch at the honey pole's foot; the lens three-quarter on him at the winch): the white RICE SYRUP flag already flies at the first band, 0.50; he walks in to the winch and cranks it and the gold HONEY flag climbs band by band past 1.00, 1.50, 2.00 to 2.17, four bands to the syrup's one; he steps back, looks from flag to flag and rubs his hands at us.

3 tuned to pass (the cheap stall's back room: plank walls, a dusty window, tied sacks of SYRUP, a steel blending vat with a big glass gauge reading HONEY at the bottom and SYRUP at the top, the syrup drum with its red SYRUP wheel, an old grey TEST box on a crate with a beacon on a post and a FAIL / PASS screen; the lens at his eye line over the bench): he dips his honey dipper in the vat and touches it to the TEST box: the beacon and the screen go red FAIL; he cranks the SYRUP wheel down a notch, dips and tests again: still red, he shakes his head; one more notch, a last test: green PASS, while the gauge still reads mostly syrup; he gapes at us.

4 the sharper test (the village hall: a tall room with a beamed ceiling, bunting from the fete, a honey-show table with rosettes on the stage, a big new white test machine with a wide funnel, a glass pipe, a round dial from green to red and a beacon on top; the lens low from the hall floor): he carries the blend that passed on his raised honey dipper and lets one drop fall into the machine's funnel; it runs down the glass pipe, the dial swings hard from PASS into FAKE, the screen lights RICE SYRUP FOUND and the beacon lights red; he jumps back and points at it.

5 almost half (the cobbled alley behind the square: brick walls, a drainpipe, a tall steel rack of the stall's imported jars, three shelves of seven, one red SUSPECT in every seven from the old test; the new EU TEST scanner on a blue rail along the rack's top with its big red lever at the foot; the lens three-quarter on him beside the rack): he hauls the lever down with both hands; the scanner's red bar sweeps the shelves and two more jars in every seven spin round to red SUSPECT, three in seven, almost half, three times the old count; he points along the reds, then turns to us with his hands out: what's in your jar?

world.logline: On market day a village beekeeper catches one fake jar in seven at the cheap stall, learns why faking pays and how the fakers tune their syrup to pass the tests, then watches the EU's sharper test catch almost half of the stall's stock.
world.hero: Data as the village's beekeeper: his lab coat under a wide beekeeper's hat with its veil rolled up round the crown, a wooden honey dipper always in his hand
world.goal: find out how much of the cheap stall's honey is really fake
world.place: one hill village in the sun: the market square with its striped stalls, his wooden honey house, the cheap stall's back room, the village hall where the inspectors set up, and the cobbled alley behind the square
world.time: one market day, from the morning market to the afternoon
world.weather: a clear warm summer day, bright sun throughout, long soft shadows by the afternoon
